subject: Biology
title: Genetics
outline: Define genetics and key terms: gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, dominance
Describe chromosomes, DNA and RNA structure and replication
Explain transcription, translation and the genetic code
State and apply Mendel's laws using monohybrid and dihybrid crosses
Explain test crosses, incomplete dominance, multiple alleles and blood group inheritance
Describe sex determination, sex linkage and applications of genetics

modules.title: Chromosomes, DNA and Protein Synthesis
modules.html:
1. Basic Terms

  • Gene – a segment of DNA coding for a polypeptide or character.
  • Allele – alternative form of a gene at the same locus.
  • Genotype – genetic make-up (e.g. Tt); phenotype – observable character (tall).
  • Homozygous (TT, tt) vs heterozygous (Tt); dominant allele masks the recessive.
  • Haploid (n) gametes, diploid (2n) body cells; humans have \(2n = 46\).

2. Nucleic Acids

DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel polynucleotide strands. Each nucleotide has deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. Complementary base pairing follows Chargaff’s rule: adenine pairs with thymine (2 hydrogen bonds) and guanine with cytosine (3 hydrogen bonds), so \( A = T \) and \( G = C \).

FeatureDNARNA
SugarDeoxyriboseRibose
BasesA, T, G, CA, U, G, C
StrandsDouble helixSingle
LocationNucleus (also mitochondria, chloroplast)Nucleus and cytoplasm
RoleStores hereditary informationmRNA, tRNA and rRNA in protein synthesis

Replication is semi-conservative: the helix unwinds, each strand acts as a template and DNA polymerase builds a complementary strand, so each daughter molecule has one old and one new strand.

3. Protein Synthesis

  1. Transcription (nucleus): RNA polymerase copies one DNA strand into messenger RNA; the mRNA leaves through a nuclear pore.
  2. Translation (ribosome): each mRNA codon of three bases is read; tRNA with the complementary anticodon brings the specific amino acid; peptide bonds join the amino acids until a stop codon is reached.

The genetic code is a triplet code, universal, degenerate (several codons per amino acid) and non-overlapping. For a polypeptide of \(n\) amino acids the coding mRNA requires \(3n\) bases.

examples.q: A DNA strand reads TAC GGA TTC. Give the mRNA and the number of amino acids coded.
examples.a: mRNA is complementary with U replacing T: AUG CCU AAG. Three codons code for three amino acids (methionine–proline–lysine); AUG is also the start codon.

examples.q: A DNA sample contains 22 % adenine. Find the percentage of guanine.
examples.a: By Chargaff's rule \(A = T = 22\%\), so \(A + T = 44\%\). Therefore \(G + C = 56\%\) and \(G = C = 28\%\).

modules.title: Mendelian Genetics
modules.html:
1. Mendel’s Laws

  • Law of segregation (first law): the two alleles of a character separate during gamete formation so that each gamete carries only one.
  • Law of independent assortment (second law): alleles of different genes are distributed to gametes independently of one another (for genes on different chromosomes).

2. Monohybrid Cross

Tall (TT) × short (tt) gives an \(F_1\) that is all Tt (tall). Selfing the \(F_1\):

Tt
TTTTt
tTttt

Genotypic ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt; phenotypic ratio 3 tall : 1 short.

3. Dihybrid Cross

RRYY × rryy gives \(F_1\) RrYy; the \(F_2\) phenotypic ratio is 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, confirming independent assortment.

4. Test Cross and Back Cross

Crossing an organism of dominant phenotype with the homozygous recessive reveals its genotype: all offspring dominant means homozygous, a 1 : 1 ratio means heterozygous.

5. Departures from Simple Dominance

  • Incomplete dominance: red × white Mirabilis gives pink \(F_1\) and a 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white \(F_2\).
  • Codominance: both alleles expressed, as in blood group AB and roan cattle.
  • Multiple alleles: ABO blood groups controlled by \(I^A\), \(I^B\) and \(i\), where \(I^A\) and \(I^B\) are codominant and both dominant over \(i\).
  • Lethal genes, epistasis and polygenic inheritance also modify ratios.

6. Sex Determination and Sex Linkage

In humans the female is XX and the male XY; the sperm determines sex, giving an expected 1 : 1 ratio. Genes on the X chromosome (haemophilia, red–green colour blindness) show sex linkage: they appear more often in males, who need only one recessive allele because they are hemizygous. Carrier mothers (XᴴXʰ) pass the allele to half their sons.

examples.q: A heterozygous black guinea pig (Bb) is crossed with a white one (bb). State the offspring ratio.
examples.a: Gametes B, b × b, b give Bb, Bb, bb, bb — a 1 : 1 ratio of black to white. This is a test cross, and the appearance of white offspring proves the black parent is heterozygous.

examples.q: A man of blood group AB marries a woman of group O. What blood groups are possible in their children?
examples.a: Father is \(I^AI^B\), mother \(ii\). Offspring are \(I^Ai\) (group A) or \(I^Bi\) (group B) in a 1 : 1 ratio. No child can be group AB or group O.

modules.title: Applications and Human Genetics
modules.html:
1. Human Genetic Disorders

DisorderNatureNote
Sickle cell anaemiaRecessive gene \(Hb^S\)AA normal, AS carrier (some malaria resistance), SS sickler
HaemophiliaX-linked recessiveBlood fails to clot; mostly males
Colour blindnessX-linked recessiveCannot distinguish red from green
AlbinismAutosomal recessiveNo melanin pigment
Down syndromeTrisomy 21 (non-disjunction)47 chromosomes

Genetic counselling before marriage, especially AS × AS couples who risk a 25 % chance of an SS child, helps prevent avoidable suffering.

2. Applications of Genetics

  • Agriculture: selective breeding, hybridisation and hybrid vigour, disease- and drought-resistant crops, artificial insemination, improved yields.
  • Medicine: genetic counselling, insulin and vaccines from genetically engineered bacteria, gene therapy.
  • Forensics and law: DNA fingerprinting for identification, paternity disputes and crime investigation.
  • Industry: enzymes, antibiotics and biofuels from engineered micro-organisms.

3. Variations in Chromosome Behaviour

Linkage occurs when genes lie on the same chromosome and tend to be inherited together, reducing the expected independent assortment ratios; crossing over can separate them, and the frequency of recombination is used to map genes.

examples.q: Two AS parents marry. Show the probability of a sickle-cell child.
examples.a: AS × AS gives AA : AS : AS : SS, that is 1 AA : 2 AS : 1 SS. The chance of a child with sickle cell anaemia (SS) is \(1/4 = 25\%\), and 50 % will be healthy carriers.

examples.q: Why is haemophilia commoner in men than in women?
examples.a: The gene is carried on the X chromosome. A man (XY) has only one X, so a single recessive allele is expressed. A woman needs two copies (one from each parent) to be affected; with one copy she is only a carrier, which is statistically far less likely.
